rows.subtype: Approach: resource and budget planning with fixed-cost-first split [Thinking]
rows.description: A new graduate with a Rs 30,000 monthly salary lists rent, food, transport and the phone bill first, then sees what remains. Working from the unavoidable costs shows how little is truly free to spend.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, planning fallacy, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: pay-yourself-first automation using a standing instruction [Action]
rows.description: On salary day the graduate sets an auto-transfer of a fixed amount to a separate savings account and a small SIP, before spending anything. Saving becomes a default rather than a daily decision.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, planning fallacy, resource and budget planning, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: spend freely and see what is left [Pitfall]
rows.description: A first-job employee treats the credited amount as abundant, buys a phone on EMI and eats out often, and finds the account empty by the 20th. The plan fails because no total was ever set against the month.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, planning fallacy, resource and budget planning, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: track spending for a month, then set category limits [Revision]
rows.description: After running short, the employee notes every UPI payment for a month, sees food delivery is the largest leak, and sets a weekly cap. Evidence from real data replaces a guessed budget.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, planning fallacy, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: copying a friend's budget percentages [Pitfall]
rows.description: A young analyst adopts a popular 50-30-20 rule from a video without noticing that sending money home and paying for shared housing make the split unrealistic. Borrowed rules fail when they ignore personal obligations.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, planning fallacy, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: buffer planning with an emergency fund target [Thinking]
rows.description: The employee decides the first goal is one month of expenses set aside, then three, before any investing. Slack absorbs surprises such as a medical bill so that a shock does not become a loan.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: negotiation, planning fallacy, resource and budget planning, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: envelope-style split into separate accounts [Action]
rows.description: The salary is divided the same day into a bills account, a spending wallet and a savings pot. When the spending wallet is empty, the person waits for next month instead of dipping into other pots.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, planning fallacy, resource and budget planning, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: values-first planning about family obligations [Thinking]
rows.description: A first-job earner decides that a fixed monthly amount for parents and a younger sibling's tuition comes before lifestyle spending. Naming what matters most makes the remaining trade-offs easier to accept.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, planning fallacy, resource and budget planning

rows.subtype: Approach: review every quarter and adjust for raises and rent hikes [Revision]
rows.description: After an appraisal and a rent increase, the employee reopens the budget, raises the savings transfer by half of the raise and trims subscriptions. The plan is treated as something to update, not a fixed contract.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, planning fallacy, values-first planning

rows.subtype: Approach: planning fallacy about irregular expenses [Pitfall]
rows.description: The budget covers monthly costs but ignores annual items such as insurance premium, festival gifts and a laptop repair. Two such bills in one quarter break the plan, showing that leaving out lumpy costs makes budgets look better than they are.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: buffer and slack, negotiation, resource and budget planning, values-first planning
